title: Mandodari's lament
hook: Ravana's queen walks onto the battlefield, and says what no one else could say
carry: mastering the senses is never done once

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Aditya Hridayam. A tired Rama turned to the sun, and one arrow ended the war. Turn to the sun.

When the noise of victory dies down, the gates of Lanka open, and the women of Ravana's palace come out onto the battlefield. They've lost husbands, sons, brothers. They walk among the dead, weeping, until they find him. One of them comes forward and kneels by the body. She is Mandodari, Ravana's chief queen, Indrajit's mother. She has lost her son, and now her husband. Valmiki lets her speak over him at length.
screen: `THE GATES OPEN.` → `THE WOMEN COME OUT.` → `MANDODARI KNEELS.`

segments.voice: Her lament holds love and truth at the same time. She remembers who he was. You frightened the gods, she says; the earth and the mountains trembled at your name. How could a man on foot, wandering in the forest, bring you down? First she answers that Rama can't be only a man; he must be Vishnu himself, come in human form. A queen of Lanka says it out loud, over her husband's body. Then she names Ravana's own part, gently and without flinching. Long ago, she says, you conquered your senses, and with that discipline you conquered the three worlds. Now it's as if your senses remembered, and took their revenge. Your desire for Sita did what no army could. This is one of Hinduism's most repeated teachings. The Upanishads picture the senses, the indriyas, as strong horses pulling the chariot of the body, and the Bhagavad Gita warns that the restless senses can carry off the mind even of a wise person who is striving. Mastery isn't won once and kept. It's one reason many Hindus keep vrats, small fasts and vows, again and again: practice in holding the reins. Ravana's tapas was legendary, and he stopped holding them. Then Mandodari simply grieves: her husband, her son, her life in pieces. Later tradition honored her among the five women, the panchakanya, whose remembrance is said to wash away wrongdoing. She saw him whole, and mourned him anyway.
screen: `YOU FRIGHTENED THE GODS.` · `RAMA IS MORE THAN A MAN.` · `YOUR SENSES TOOK REVENGE.` · `THE SENSES ARE STRONG HORSES.` · then, large: `MASTERY IS NEVER DONE ONCE.` · `ONE OF THE FIVE WOMEN.`

segments.voice: Many Hindus keep a vrat, a small vow of holding back, on a set day. Try a tiny one now: choose one thing you'll go without today, a snack, a scroll, a second helping. If you pray, offer it to God; if you don't, just notice the pull when it comes, and hold the reins for one breath longer.
Mandodari. Ravana's chief queen and Indrajit's mother, who grieves him on the battlefield, naming both his greatness and the senses that took their revenge.
Your line: mastering the senses is never done once. The king still lies on the field, waiting for his last rites. See you then.

howItsDone: Some Hindus recite a traditional verse naming five revered women of the epics, the pañcakanyā, with Mandodari among them, and some say it in the morning; versions differ on one of the names.

Mandodari.meaning: Ravana's chief queen and Indrajit's mother

Vishnu.meaning: the god Mandodari says Rama must be, in human form

vrat.meaning: a vow, often a fast, kept on set days

panchakanya.meaning: the five revered women of the epics

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda 110–111 (the women of Lanka come out; Mandodari's lament)
The pañcakanyā verse (ahalyā draupadī sītā tārā mandodarī tathā)
Bhagavad Gita 2.60 (the restless senses carry off the mind even of a wise person who strives)
Katha Upanishad 1.3.3–4 (the chariot image: the senses are the horses)

notes: Sarga numbers follow the common (vulgate) numbering; confirm.
Mandodari's identification of Rama as Vishnu, the eternal supreme self (often cited as vyaktam eṣa mahāyogī paramātmā sanātanaḥ): paraphrased; confirm.
The senses-taking-revenge image (indriyāṇi purā jitvā jitaṃ tribhuvanaṃ tvayā / smaradbhir iva tad vairam indriyair eva nirjitaḥ): paraphrased; confirm.
The pañcakanyā verse: versions vary (Sita or Kunti); the script says only that Mandodari is among the five.
The meaning of the name Mandodarī ('slender-waisted'): confirm.
